ref: De viris illustribus 25 (Jerome, Richardson's translation chapter 25)
greek_edition: Latin not read (Jerome De viris, Migne PL 23 not opened)
english: Theophilus, sixth bishop of the church of Antioch, in the reign of the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus composed a book Against Marcion, which is still extant, also three volumes To Autolycus and one Against the heresy of Hermogenes and other short and elegant treatises, well fitted for the edification of the church. I have read, under his name, commentaries On the Gospel and On the proverbs of Solomon which do not appear to me to correspond in style and language with the elegance and expressiveness of the above works.
page: page unknown (newadvent page has no page numbers)
edition: NPNF2 vol. 3, ed. Schaff & Wace (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892)
what_it_says: Jerome says Theophilus wrote a book Against Marcion (which he calls still extant), three books To Autolycus, and an anti-Hermogenes work, and that he himself read Gospel and Proverbs commentaries under Theophilus's name but doubted their style.
limits: Jerome does not discuss the Trinity; his 'still extant' Against Marcion is not among the surviving works (Ad Autolycum is the only extant work); his doubts concern style, not doctrine.

greek_edition: Greek not read (Schwartz GCS edition not opened)
english: At that time also in the church of Antioch, Theophilus was well known as the sixth from the apostles. For Cornelius, who succeeded Hero, was the fourth, and after him Eros, the fifth in order, had held the office of bishop.
page: page unknown (newadvent page has no page numbers)
edition: NPNF2 vol. 1, ed. Schaff & Wace (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1890)
what_it_says: Eusebius places Theophilus as the sixth bishop of Antioch from the apostles, after Cornelius and Eros.
limits: Only succession context; no doctrinal content.

greek_edition: Greek not read
english: Of Theophilus, whom we have mentioned as bishop of the church of Antioch, three elementary works addressed to Autolycus are extant; also another writing entitled Against the Heresy of Hermogenes, in which he makes use of testimonies from the Apocalypse of John, and finally certain other catechetical books.
edition: NPNF2 vol. 1 (1890)
what_it_says: Eusebius knows three elementary books To Autolycus, a work Against the Heresy of Hermogenes using Apocalypse testimony, and other catechetical books.
limits: Eusebius's list does not include a work On the Trinity or a work on the Spirit; it confirms the Apocalypse-based Hermogenes work, which is lost.

greek_edition: Greek not read
english: And that Theophilus also, with the others, contended against them, is manifest from a certain discourse of no common merit written by him against Marcion. This work too, with the others of which we have spoken, has been preserved to the present day.
edition: NPNF2 vol. 1 (1890)
what_it_says: Eusebius says Theophilus wrote a discourse against Marcion and that it was still preserved in his day.
limits: The Marcion discourse is not among the surviving works; Eusebius's 'preserved' claim is not checkable from the surviving corpus.

greek_edition: Latin not read
english: Theophilus, [108] in his book written to Autolycus respecting the times, [109] says that Thallus relates in his history, that Belus, who is worshipped by the Babylonians and Assyrians, is found to have lived 322 years before the Trojan war; that Belus, moreover, was contemporary with Saturnus, and that they both grew up at one time;-- [excerpt]
edition: ANF vol. 7 (Roberts & Donaldson, American reprint of the Edinburgh edition); text read on ccel.org
what_it_says: Lactantius cites Theophilus on chronology, quoting his book to Autolycus 'respecting the times'; the ANF editor's footnote says no extant Theophilus work has that title.
limits: A chronological citation only; the editor's footnote [109] is the ANF annotator, not Lactantius. No Trinitarian content here.

greek: Haec vis et haec divini sensus dispositio, apud Scripturas etiam in Sophiae nomine ostenditur. Quid enim sapientius ratione Dei, sive sermone? Itaque Sophiam quoque exaudi, ut secundam personam conditam. Primo, Dominus (Prov. VIII, 22) creavit me initium viarum in opera sua, priusquam terram faceret, priusquam montes collocarentur: ante omnes autem colles generavit me; in sensu suo scilicet condens et generans. Dehinc assistentem eam ipsa separatione cognosce; Cum pararet , inquit, coelum, aderam illi simul ; et cum fortia faciebat super ventos quae sursum nubila; et cum tutos ponebat fontes ejus quae sub coelo, ego eram cum illo compingens; ego eram ad quam gaudebat: quotidie autem oblectabar in persona ipsius . Nam ut primum Deus voluit ea quae cum sophiae ratione et sermone disposuerat intra se, in substantias et species suas edere, ipsum primum protulit sermonem, habentem in se individuas suas, Rationem et Sophiam; ut per ipsum fierent universa, per quem erant cogitata atque disposita; imo et facta jam, quantum in Dei sensu. Hoc enim eis deerat, ut coram quoque in suis speciebus atque substantiis cognoscerentur et tenerentur.
greek_edition: Latin: Migne PL 2 cols. 161-162 as printed on earlychurchtexts.com (not an original PL scan; text one word per line, rejoined)
english: Listen therefore to Wisdom herself, constituted in the character of a Second Person: At the first the Lord created me as the beginning of His ways, with a view to His own works, before He made the earth, before the mountains were settled; moreover, before all the hills did He beget me; Proverbs 8:22-25 that is to say, He created and generated me in His own intelligence.
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo 1885)
what_it_says: Tertullian, the first Latin writer to name Wisdom as a second Person, says God 'created and generated' Wisdom in His own intelligence, before the hills.
limits: Tertullian does not name Theophilus; the Latin reads 'creavit' in ch. 6 (Botte and Evans dispute the reading, per search snippets only). Wisdom is not yet the Holy Spirit here.

greek: Tunc igitur etiam ipse sermo speciem et ornatum suum sumit, sonum et vocem, cum dicit Deus: Fiat lux . Haec est nativitas perfecta sermonis, dum ex Deo procedit: conditus ab eo primum ab cogitatum in nomine Sophiae: Dominus condidit me initium viarum . Dehinc generatus ad effectum:
greek_edition: Latin: Migne PL 2 cols. 161-162 as printed on earlychurchtexts.com (rejoined from the one-word-per-line page)
english: This is the perfect nativity of the Word, when He proceeds forth from God — formed by Him first to devise and think out all things under the name of Wisdom — The Lord created or formed me as the beginning of His ways; Proverbs 8:22 then afterward begotten, to carry all into effect
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo 1885)
what_it_says: Tertullian calls the Word's going forth from God a 'perfect nativity', quoting Prov 8:22 (English 'created or formed me'; Latin 'condidit me') before the Word is 'begotten to carry all into effect'.
limits: The Latin 'condidit' (ch. 7) and 'creavit' (ch. 6) differ; this is the Latin form of the Theophilus-style 'going forth at a point' problem. Tertullian is not Theophilus and does not cite him.

ref: De Synodis §8 (Athanasius, Sirmium creed of 351, quoted by Athanasius)
greek_edition: Greek not read; English NPNF2 text read
english: And in one Only-begotten Son of God, who, before all ages, and before all origin, and before all conceivable time, and before all comprehensible essence, was begotten impassibly from God: through whom the ages were disposed and all things were made;
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson
edition: NPNF2 vol. 4, ed. Schaff & Wace (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892)
what_it_says: The 'Catholic Faith' published at Sirmium in 351, which Athanasius reports as put forward by the Arian-party bishops, calls the Son begotten 'before all origin' and 'before all conceivable time'. It cites no Theophilus.
limits: No Theophilus citation anywhere in De Synodis (the only 'Theophil' hit is Theophronius of Tyana). The creed is not a Theophilus witness; the Greek is not read.

ref: Newman's note on p. 214 (Athanasius De Decretis note on 'prin gennethenai ouk en'), para. 1
greek_edition: English (Newman's note); Greek not script
english: Now five early writers, Athenagoras, Tatian, Theophilus, Hippolytus, and Novatian, of whom the authority of Hippolytus is very great, not to speak of Theophilus and Athenagoras, whatever be thought of Tatian and of Novatian, seem to speak of the divine generation as taking place immediately before the creation of the world
edition: Newman, Treatises of St. Athanasius (Library of the Fathers), note on p. 214; newmanreader.org copy
what_it_says: Newman says five early writers, including Theophilus, seem to put the divine generation immediately before creation, which he reads as 'not eternal' and against Bull's reading.
limits: Newman's own reading, not Theophilus's words. He counts Theophilus among five writers and says Bull's answer must be shown to fit the text.

ref: Ad Autolycum 2.10-22 (quoted in Newman's note, Greek in Latin letters)
greek: [Echon ouk ho theos ton heautou logon endiatheton en tois idiois splanchnois, egennesen auton meta tes heautou sophias exereuxamenos pro ton holon … hopote de ethelesen ho theos poiesai hosa ebouleusato, touton ton logon egennese prophorikon, prototokon pases ktiseos].
greek_edition: Newman's transliteration into Latin letters of the Greek (not a Greek-script edition)
edition: Newman, Treatises of St. Athanasius (Library of the Fathers), note on p. 214
what_it_says: Newman quotes Theophilus's 'the Word the Father begot, uttering Him, the first-born of all creation' in transliterated Greek.
limits: The Greek is Newman's transliteration; the Greek script is not reproduced here and must be checked against Otto (1861) or Grant (1970). The English given is only Newman's.

work: Defensio Fidei Nicaenae (Bull, as quoted by Newman)
ref: Defensio Fidei Nicaenae III.9 §2 (Bull's Latin, quoted by Newman p. 278)
greek: Catholici quidam Doctores, qui post exortam controversiam Arianam vixerunt, ... illam [tou logou] … ex Patre progressionem (quam et [sunkatabasin], hoc est, condescensionem eorum nonnulli appell�runt), ad condendum h�c universa agnovere; atque ejus etiam progressionis respectu
greek_edition: Latin as quoted in Newman's note (source shows a garbled character at 'appell...runt'); Bull's Latin not opened in the original
edition: Bull, Defensio Fidei Nicaenae (1685), as quoted by Newman, Treatises of St. Athanasius note on p. 214
what_it_says: Bull says some Catholic doctors after Arius spoke of a 'progressio' of the Word (sunkatabasis) by which He was born from God before the creation, which he reads as metaphorical.
limits: Bull's argument is known here only through Newman's quotation; the original (Oxford 1851-52 edition, Defensio III.5-9) has not been opened.

ref: NPNF2 vol. 4 editorial note [931] (Athanasius De Decretis passage 'ek tes hypostaseos')
greek_edition: English editorial note; no Greek script
english: [931] The word trias, usually translated Trinity, is first used by Theophilus, ad Autol. ii. 15.
page: page unknown (ccel text has no page numbers)
edition: NPNF2 vol. 4, ed. Schaff & Wace (1892); read on ccel.org plain text
what_it_says: The editor says that 'trias', usually translated Trinity, is first used by Theophilus, Ad Autolycum 2.15.
limits: A secondary note: the word 'trias' is confirmed in 2.15 (Dods's English reads 'Trinity'); the claim is an editor's, not Theophilus's own statement about the word's novelty.

ref: NPNF2 vol. 4 Prolegomena (introduction to Athanasius, on Tertullian's Trinitas)
greek_edition: English introduction; no Greek script
english: which he is the first to use (trias first in the Asiatic Apologist Theophilus).
edition: NPNF2 vol. 4 (1892); read on ccel.org plain text
what_it_says: The introduction says Tertullian was the first to use 'Trinitas', while the Asiatic apologist Theophilus used 'trias' earlier.
limits: Secondary; it rests on the same ad Autol. 2.15 point.

ref: NPNF2 vol. 4 Prolegomena on the Apologists (endiathetos / prophorikos)
greek_edition: English introduction; no Greek script
english: Before this He was the logos endiathetos, after it the logos prophorikos, the Word uttered (Ps. xlv. 1 LXX; this distinction is not in Justin, but is found Theophil. ad Autol. ii. 10, 22: it is the most marked trace of philosophic [Stoic] influence on the Apologists
edition: NPNF2 vol. 4 (1892); read on ccel.org plain text
what_it_says: The introduction says Theophilus gives the Word the endiathetos/prophorikos distinction, the most marked Stoic trace among the Apologists.
limits: Secondary; the editor's judgement of Stoic influence is not Theophilus's statement.

ref: NPNF2 vol. 4 editorial note [3555] (Athanasius, cross-referenced to De Decr. §10)
greek_edition: English editorial note; no Greek script
english: S. Theophilus speaks of our Lord as at once endiathetos and prophorikos. ad Autol. ii. 10 and 22
edition: NPNF2 vol. 4 (1892); read on ccel.org plain text
what_it_says: The note says Theophilus speaks of the Lord as both endiathetos and prophorikos (Ad Autolycum 2.10 and 2.22), and that the distinction was allowed in Catholic theology under limits.
limits: The note concedes the distinction only with limits (Damascene, FO ii.21 cited); it is a secondary note, not a Nicene decision.

greek_edition: Greek not read (Otto 1861 / Grant 1970 not opened)
english: God, then, having His own Word internal within His own bowels, begot Him, emitting Him along with His own wisdom before all things.
edition: ANF vol. 2 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo 1885)
what_it_says: Theophilus says God begot His internal Word, emitting Him along with His wisdom before all things, and used Him as helper in creation.
limits: This is the passage behind the 'begotten at a point' objection; the English is Dods's, not verbatim Greek. Greek and the endiathetos/prophorikos terms are not read here.

greek_edition: Greek not read
english: He, then, being Spirit of God, and governing principle, and wisdom, and power of the highest, came down upon the prophets ... came down upon the prophets
edition: ANF vol. 2 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo 1885)
what_it_says: In the same chapter Theophilus gives the Spirit of God the titles 'governing principle, and wisdom, and power of the highest'.
limits: This is the 'Wisdom and Spirit used interchangeably' passage; the Holy Spirit is not separated from the Word here.

greek_edition: Greek not read
english: In like manner also the three days which were before the luminaries, are types of the Trinity, of God, and His Word, and His wisdom.
edition: ANF vol. 2 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo 1885)
what_it_says: The three days before the luminaries are types of the Trinity: God, His Word, and His wisdom.
limits: Dods translates 'Trinity' where the Greek is 'trias' (per the NPNF2 note); the triad is God, Word, Wisdom, with no separate Holy Spirit.

greek_edition: Greek not read
english: But when God wished to make all that He determined on, He begot this Word, uttered, the first-born of all creation, not Himself being emptied of the Word [Reason], but having begotten Reason, and always conversing with His Reason.
edition: ANF vol. 2 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo 1885)
what_it_says: God begot the Word, uttered, as firstborn of all creation, while Himself not being emptied of Reason; the Word had always resided in God's heart.
limits: The sequence 'begot ... uttered' gives the temporal-generation objection; Theophilus states the Word is 'always' present, which the Newman and Bull dispute turns on.

greek_edition: Greek not read
english: But what else is this voice but the Word of God, who is also His Son? Not as the poets and writers of myths talk of the sons of gods begotten from intercourse [with women], but as truth expounds, the Word, that always exists, residing within the heart of God.
edition: ANF vol. 2 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo 1885)
what_it_says: Theophilus identifies the voice Adam heard as 'the Word of God, who is also His Son'.
limits: Here 'Son' is a title for the Word who walks in Paradise in God's person; Theophilus never uses homoousios, and the passage is one of the few places he says 'Son'.

ref: Jerome, Epistula 121 (Ad Algasiam), as quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia article on Theophilus
greek: Theophilus . . . quattuor Evangelistarum in unum opus compingens
greek_edition: Latin not read; newadvent Letter 121 page holds only the eleven questions
edition: Catholic Encyclopedia vol. 14 (1912)
what_it_says: Jerome says Theophilus composed a Gospel harmony; a long quotation from it survives in Ep. 121 according to the CE.
limits: Secondary citation only; the Latin quotation has not been read in a primary edition. The Gospel harmony is not the Ad Autolycum.
